title: Most of the Universe Is Missing
hook: Everything we can see adds up to about a twentieth of what is out there.
story: Galaxies spin, and how fast the outer parts spin should depend on how much mass is pulling on them. In the Solar System this works neatly: distant planets orbit slowly, close ones quickly, exactly as gravity predicts from the Sun's mass. Galaxies refuse to behave. Their outer stars move nearly as fast as their inner ones, which means far more mass must be pulling than anything we can see provides.

Astronomers call the missing material dark matter, which is an honest name rather than a clever one: dark because it emits no light at all, matter because it has gravity. It does not glow, does not block light, does not appear to react chemically with anything, and passes through ordinary matter as though it were not there. It appears to outweigh everything visible in the universe by roughly five to one.

There is more than one line of evidence. Dark matter bends light passing near it, so astronomers can map where it sits by watching distant galaxies appear smeared and duplicated. The pattern of faint heat left over from the Big Bang also carries its fingerprint. And computer simulations of how galaxies formed only produce a universe resembling ours if the extra mass is included.

Enormous effort has gone into catching a single particle of it. Detectors sit deep underground, shielded by kilometres of rock to block everything else, waiting for one dark matter particle to nudge one atom. Decades of increasingly sensitive searches have found nothing definite. Either the particle is stranger or lighter than the leading guesses, or — a minority view, but a serious one — our understanding of gravity itself needs modifying at galactic scales. Meanwhile, dark matter may be streaming through your body as you read this, without touching a single atom of you.
wow: Dark matter may be streaming through your body right now, without touching a single atom of you.

quiz.q: Why do scientists think dark matter exists?
a: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible mass
They have seen it in telescopes

quiz.q: Has anyone detected a dark matter particle?
a: Not yet, despite decades of searching

title: Nobody Knows Why We Sleep
hook: You will spend about a third of your life doing something science cannot fully explain.
story: Sleep looks, on the face of it, like a terrible idea. An animal lying still for hours cannot eat, cannot watch for danger, cannot defend its territory and cannot reproduce. Evolution is ruthless about waste, so whatever sleep provides must be worth that enormous cost. And essentially every animal examined properly does some version of it, including insects, fish, worms and even jellyfish, which have no brain at all.

There are good partial answers. Memories are strengthened and reorganised during sleep — people who sleep after learning something perform far better than people who do not, and researchers can watch the day's patterns replay in a sleeping brain. Waste products are cleared from brain tissue more effectively during sleep. Growth hormone is released, tissue is repaired, and the immune system works better afterwards.

None of that quite explains the price, though. A resting animal could do most of those things without switching off its awareness of a dangerous world. Something about sleep appears to require genuine disconnection, and nobody can say precisely what.

What is clear is that going without it is catastrophic. Sleep-deprived people hallucinate and lose the ability to think straight within days. In animal experiments, total deprivation eventually kills, faster than starvation does, and researchers still cannot identify exactly what runs out or fails first. After more than a century of study, the honest summary is that we know a great deal about what happens during sleep and still cannot say what it is fundamentally for. Dolphins, incidentally, sleep one half of the brain at a time, so they never stop swimming or surfacing to breathe.
wow: Dolphins sleep one half of the brain at a time, so they never stop swimming or surfacing to breathe.

quiz.q: What happens to memories during sleep?
How well do scientists understand why we sleep?
a: Partly — the core reason is still unknown

title: How Did Life Start?
hook: Chemistry became something that copies itself, and nobody knows how.
story: For its first few hundred million years, Earth had no life on it at all — just rock, water, gases and a great deal of energy from volcanoes, lightning and an unshielded Sun. Then, somehow, chemistry crossed a line and became biology. The earliest widely accepted traces of living things are around 3.5 billion years old, and disputed hints go back further, which suggests life appeared relatively quickly once conditions allowed it.

The first steps are demonstrably possible. In 1953 a graduate student named Stanley Miller sealed water and simple gases in glassware, ran electric sparks through it to imitate lightning, and found amino acids — the building blocks of proteins — forming within days. It caused a sensation. Since then, similar molecules have been found in meteorites and detected in clouds of gas between the stars, so the raw ingredients are evidently common.

The hard part is what comes next. Building blocks are not life. Life requires something that copies itself, with mistakes rare enough for the copies to stay useful and common enough to allow change over time. One leading idea is that RNA came first, because it can both carry information like DNA and act as a machine like a protein, which would remove the chicken-and-egg problem of needing one to make the other.

Where it happened is argued about as fiercely as how. Candidates include hot alkaline vents on the deep sea floor, shallow pools that repeatedly dried and refilled, and surfaces of clay minerals that could hold molecules in place. Nobody has yet built life from scratch in a laboratory, though researchers keep getting closer to individual pieces. What is not in doubt is the result: every living thing on Earth, from a whale to a mushroom to you, appears to descend from a single common beginning.
wow: Every living thing on Earth, from a whale to a mushroom to you, appears to descend from the same single beginning.

quiz.q: What did the Miller experiment produce?
a: Amino acids, the building blocks of proteins

quiz.q: What is the hard unsolved step?

title: Why Does Anything Feel Like Anything?
hook: Science can explain what your brain does, but not why it feels like something to be you.
story: Scientists can follow a signal from your eye through several stages of your brain, watch which regions become active, and predict a surprising amount about what you will notice and do next. Brain scanners can sometimes tell which of two pictures a person is looking at. All of this is machinery, and it is being mapped steadily.

None of it explains the part that seems most obvious to you: that there is something it is like to see red, to taste mango, to feel worried. A camera processes light without, as far as anyone can tell, any experience accompanying it. Why is your brain different? Why does all that signal processing not simply happen in the dark?

The philosopher David Chalmers named this the hard problem in 1995, separating it from the merely very difficult problems of working out what the brain does. The distinction matters because progress on the difficult problems does not obviously chip away at the hard one. You could in principle map every neuron and still be left asking why the map is accompanied by a point of view.

Serious proposals exist and disagree completely. One holds that experience arises when information is broadcast widely across the brain, becoming available to many systems at once. Another argues it depends on how densely interconnected a system is, and proposes a number that measures it — which would imply some very simple systems have a flicker of experience. Others think the question is confused and will dissolve once neuroscience is finished, the way the search for a life force did. No experiment yet distinguishes between them, which is unusual in modern science. And nobody can prove that anyone else is conscious at all: you only ever have direct evidence of your own.
wow: Nobody can prove that anyone else is conscious — you only ever have direct evidence of your own experience.

quiz.q: What is the hard problem?
a: Why brain activity feels like anything

quiz.q: Do scientists agree on an answer?

title: We Have Better Maps of Mars
hook: Most of the sea floor has never been seen by anyone.
story: The ocean covers more than two-thirds of the planet, and most of it is deep, dark and cold. Mapping it properly is slow work: satellites can only sense the sea floor indirectly, through tiny bumps in the shape of the sea surface caused by gravity, which gives a blurry picture. Sharp detail requires a ship to pass overhead sounding the bottom, and ships are slow and expensive.

So although rough maps cover every ocean, only around a quarter of the sea floor has been measured at modern resolution. We have better maps of the surfaces of the Moon and Mars, simply because photographing an airless world from orbit is easier than seeing through four kilometres of water. An international effort is working to map the whole sea floor properly, and it is not finished.

The living space down there is the largest on Earth, and barely sampled. Below the depth sunlight reaches, animals rely on food drifting down from above or on chemical energy from vents. Most creatures in the deep can make their own light, and use it to lure prey, to signal, and to hide by matching the faint glow from above. Nearly every expedition with a modern camera records animals nobody has described.

Getting there remains genuinely hard. Pressure at the bottom of the deepest trench is over a thousand times that at the surface, enough to crush almost any vessel, and only a handful of people have ever been to the bottom of the Mariana Trench — fewer than have walked on the Moon. The giant squid, an animal known from corpses for over a century, was not filmed alive in its own habitat until 2012.
wow: The giant squid was photographed alive in its own habitat for the first time only in 2012.

quiz.q: How much of the sea floor is mapped in detail?
What can most deep-sea creatures do?

title: The Book Nobody Can Read
hook: A 600-year-old book is written in a script that no one has ever decoded.
story: The Voynich manuscript is a handwritten book of about 240 surviving pages, written in a script that matches no known writing system, and illustrated throughout. There are plants that resemble no species anyone can identify, circular diagrams that look astronomical or astrological, and strange pictures of women bathing in green pools linked by pipes and tubes. Nobody knows what a single word of it says.

It is genuinely old. Radiocarbon dating of the parchment in 2009 placed it in the early 1400s, and analysis of the inks and pigments is consistent with that period, which rules out a forgery by the book dealer Wilfrid Voynich, who bought it in 1912 and gave it its name. Its earlier history is patchy: it can be traced to the court of Rudolf II in Prague and to a seventeenth-century letter asking a scholar for help reading it. He failed too.

The text behaves in some ways like a real language. Certain symbols appear far more often than others, word lengths cluster in a natural-looking way, and there are repeated patterns of the kind languages produce. In other ways it is odd: words repeat next to each other far more often than in any known language, and the statistics differ between sections of the book.

The world's best code-breakers have tried and failed, including teams from both world wars who broke far harder military ciphers. Computers have been thrown at it repeatedly. Claimed solutions surface every few years — a lost Turkish dialect, an artificial language, shorthand Latin — and none has survived examination by other scholars. It may be a cipher, a lost or invented language, or an elaborate hoax created to sell to a wealthy collector six centuries ago. It sits in a library at Yale, and anyone can study every page online for free.
wow: It sits in a library at Yale University, and anyone can look at every page online for free.

quiz.q: How old is the manuscript?
Has anyone decoded it?
a: No — claimed solutions never hold up

title: Why Is There Anything At All?
hook: By the rules as we understand them, the universe should be empty.
story: Every kind of particle has an opposite twin, called antimatter: identical in mass, opposite in charge. This is not speculation — antimatter is made routinely in laboratories and in hospital scanners, and it behaves exactly as predicted. Bring a particle and its antiparticle together and they annihilate completely, converting entirely into energy.

That is where the problem starts. When energy turns into particles, it produces them in matched pairs, one of each. In the intense heat just after the Big Bang, enormous numbers of particles and antiparticles were created this way. If they were made in exactly equal numbers, they should have found each other and annihilated entirely, leaving a universe containing light and nothing else — no stars, no planets, nobody to be puzzled by it.

Instead there is matter everywhere and almost no antimatter. Careful measurements of the leftover glow from the early universe suggest the imbalance was tiny: roughly one extra particle of matter survived for every billion pairs that destroyed each other. Everything that exists — every star, every stone, every person — is built from that small surplus.

Experiments have found small differences in how matter and antimatter behave, particularly in certain rare particle decays, so the symmetry is not perfect. But when physicists add up the size of these known differences, they fall short of explaining a billion-to-one imbalance by an enormous margin. Something in our best theory of particles is missing. Large experiments are currently measuring antimatter in detail, including whether antihydrogen falls downwards under gravity — it does, as it happens — in the hope of finding the discrepancy that explains why there is something rather than nothing.
wow: Everything you have ever seen or touched is made of the small amount of matter that survived the destruction.

quiz.q: What happens when matter meets antimatter?
a: They destroy each other in a flash

quiz.q: What is the puzzle?
a: Why any matter survived at all

title: Why Does Time Only Go Forwards?
hook: Almost every law of physics works equally well backwards. Time does not.
story: Film a ball bouncing and play it in reverse: it looks odd but nothing is broken. The physics works either way. Nearly all fundamental laws are like this — they contain no preference for one direction of time. Yet we never see a smashed cup gather itself back together, and we remember the past rather than the future.

The best answer involves counting. There are enormously many ways for a cup to be smashed and very few ways for it to be whole, so a random jumble of atoms is overwhelmingly likely to be a mess. Physicists measure this with entropy, and the rule is that disorder tends to increase simply because disordered arrangements are more numerous.

But that only pushes the question back. If disorder increases because it is more likely, the universe must have started in an extremely ordered state — otherwise there would be nowhere to increase from. Why it began that way is unexplained, and it may be the deepest version of the question.

Time is stranger still in relativity. It runs slower for fast-moving objects and in stronger gravity, so there is no universal clock and no shared present moment. Some physicists argue that time is not a fundamental ingredient of reality at all, but something that emerges from deeper rules — a view that is taken seriously and is nowhere near settled.
wow: A clock at your feet runs very slightly slower than one at your head, and this has been measured over a height difference of a single metre.

quiz.q: Why does disorder tend to increase?
a: There are far more disordered arrangements
A force pushes it that way

quiz.q: What remains unexplained?
a: Why the universe began so ordered

discovery: Time stopped being absolute in 1905. Einstein showed that two people moving differently genuinely disagree about which events happen at the same moment, and neither is wrong. It sounded like philosophy until it was measured: in 1971 caesium clocks were flown around the world on ordinary airliners and came back disagreeing with the clock left behind, by exactly the predicted fraction of a microsecond. Satellite navigation now corrects for the same effect continuously.

title: Where Is Everybody?
hook: The galaxy is huge and old. So why has nobody called?
story: Our galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars, and we now know that planets are ordinary — most stars have them, and many have one at a comfortable distance for liquid water. The galaxy is also about 13 billion years old, so any civilisation that arose early would have had an enormous head start. Even at slow speeds, a determined species could have spread across it in a few tens of millions of years, which is quick on that scale.
The physicist Enrico Fermi is said to have summed up the problem over lunch in 1950 with a simple question: where is everybody? We have listened for radio signals since 1960 and found nothing.

Proposed answers fall into groups, and all are guesses. Perhaps life itself is extraordinarily rare. Perhaps simple life is common and complex life is not — Earth had only microbes for around three billion years. Perhaps civilisations reliably destroy themselves, or lose interest in broadcasting, or communicate in ways we cannot detect. Perhaps we have not looked at very much: the searches so far cover a tiny fraction of the sky, frequencies and time.
There is a quiet unease in the question. If the great filter that keeps the galaxy silent lies behind us, we were lucky. If it lies ahead, that is less comfortable.
wow: Our own radio signals have only reached a bubble about a hundred light years wide — a speck of the galaxy.

quiz.q: What is the Fermi paradox?
a: The galaxy is old and huge, yet seems silent

quiz.q: How much of the sky have we searched?

discovery: The listening began in 1960, when Frank Drake pointed a radio telescope at two nearby stars for a few months and heard nothing. He later wrote down an equation, not to calculate an answer but to organise the question into its parts: how many stars, how many with planets, how many with life, and so on. Most of those terms are still guesses. Two of them — how many stars have planets, and how many are in the habitable zone — have only been measured in the last twenty years.

title: Nobody Knows Why You Dream
hook: You will spend around six years of your life dreaming, and science cannot say why.
story: Dreaming is not rare or occasional. Everyone does it, several times a night, most vividly during a stage called REM sleep when the eyes flick about beneath closed lids and the brain becomes nearly as active as when awake. The body is paralysed during it, apart from eyes and breathing — a safety mechanism that stops you acting out what you are seeing.

The explanations disagree with each other. One says dreams help process emotion, taking the sting out of difficult memories by replaying them without the stress chemicals. Another says they are rehearsal — a safe simulator for threats, which would explain why being chased is such a common dream worldwide. A third says they are largely a by-product: the sleeping brain firing as it consolidates memories, and the waking mind stitching a story out of the noise afterwards.

Evidence exists for all three and settles none. People deprived of REM sleep do worse at some learning tasks, which supports a purpose. But people who lose REM sleep for years through certain medications often report no obvious harm, which does not.

There is not even agreement on whether dreams mean anything. Most researchers reject the idea that symbols carry fixed meanings, while accepting that what you dream about clearly reflects what occupies you — which is a much weaker claim, and the only one the evidence comfortably supports.
wow: Blind people dream too. Those blind from birth report dreams rich in sound, touch and smell rather than images.

quiz.q: What happens to the body during REM sleep?
Do scientists agree why we dream?

title: What Came Before the Beginning?
hook: Asking what happened before the Big Bang may be like asking what is north of the North Pole.
story: The evidence that the universe was once hot, dense and much smaller is strong: galaxies are moving apart, the leftover glow of the early heat is measurable in every direction, and the proportions of the lightest elements match what that early furnace should have produced.

Wind the expansion backwards and everything converges about 13.8 billion years ago. At that point the equations produce infinities — infinite density, infinite temperature — which is not a description of reality but a signal that the theory has stopped working. General relativity, which handles gravity, and quantum mechanics, which handles the very small, give contradictory answers in exactly the conditions where both are needed.
So the honest position is that the Big Bang describes what happened from a tiny fraction of a second onward, extremely well, and says nothing reliable about the first instant or anything before it.

The proposals are serious but untested. Perhaps time itself began then, making before a meaningless word — the North Pole answer. Perhaps our universe emerged from a previous collapsing one, or budded off from a larger structure that has always existed. Distinguishing these would need evidence from the first moments, and it is not obvious that any survives.
wow: The oldest light we can see left when the universe was about 380,000 years old. Everything earlier is hidden behind a fog.

quiz.q: What do the equations give at the very beginning?
What is the North Pole comparison about?
a: Before may be a meaningless question

discovery: The expansion was found by accident. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble measured the distances to other galaxies and noticed that the further away one was, the faster it was moving from us — which only makes sense if everything is spreading apart. Earlier, Henrietta Swan Leavitt had made this possible by discovering that certain pulsing stars reveal their true brightness through their rhythm, giving astronomers their first reliable way to measure cosmic distance. She was paid as a computer and never given a professorship.

title: Do Animals Have Language?
hook: Plenty of animals communicate. Whether any of them has language is a harder question.
story: Communication is everywhere. Bees dance directions, prairie dogs have different alarm calls for a hawk and for a human, and some appear to add detail about size and colour. Vervet monkeys have distinct warnings for eagle, snake and leopard, and respond correctly to recordings. All of that is real information passing between animals.

Language, in the strict sense linguists use, asks for more: a set of units that can be recombined by rules into an unlimited number of new meanings, including sentences about things absent, past, hypothetical or false. A child can say the dog that was not there yesterday might come tomorrow, and be understood.

Attempts to teach apes sign language produced striking results and fierce arguments. Some animals learned hundreds of signs and combined them. Critics argued the combinations were mostly imitation and prompting, and that the grammar never really appeared — a dispute that has never fully resolved, partly because the studies were hard to repeat cleanly.

Research now leans towards a different question. Instead of asking whether animals have language, ask which individual ingredients they share — memory for sequences, taking turns, learning sounds from others, referring to absent things. Several species have some. No other species is known to have all of them together, and nobody can say why.
wow: Sperm whales make patterned clicks that differ between groups, and researchers are now using machine learning to look for structure in them.

quiz.q: What does language require that calls do not?
a: Recombining units into unlimited new meanings

quiz.q: How has the research question changed?

discovery: One of the sharpest results came from prairie dogs. Con Slobodchikoff recorded their alarm calls for decades and found consistent differences depending on what was approaching, including calls that appeared to distinguish a tall human in a yellow shirt from a short human in blue. Other researchers question how much is really being encoded. The dispute is typical of the field: the recordings are real, the statistics are arguable, and animals cannot be asked what they meant.

title: Medicine That Contains Nothing
hook: A pill with no medicine in it can still make people genuinely feel better.
story: Give someone a sugar pill and tell them it is a painkiller, and a meaningful number will report less pain. This is not simply politeness or imagination. Brain scans show real changes in pain-processing regions, and the body releases its own painkilling chemicals — a response that can be blocked by a drug that blocks those chemicals, which is strong evidence something physical is happening.

The effect has rules that make no obvious sense. Injections work better than pills. Larger pills work better than small ones. Expensive-looking ones work better than cheap ones. Two pills beat one. The colour matters, and differs between countries.

Strangest of all, it can work when the patient knows. In trials where people are told plainly that they are receiving a placebo with no active ingredient, some still improve. Nobody has a satisfying explanation for that.

It has limits that matter. Placebos can change how bad something feels — pain, nausea, fatigue — but they do not shrink tumours or cure infections. That is precisely why medicines must be tested against them: if a new drug performs no better than a sugar pill, it is not working. The effect is also why honest trials hide from both patient and doctor which is which.
wow: There is an opposite effect too. Warn people of a side effect and some will experience it from a pill containing nothing.

quiz.q: Is the placebo effect only imagination?
a: No — measurable changes occur in the body

quiz.q: What can placebos not do?

discovery: The word comes from a Latin phrase meaning I shall please, and for centuries it described a doctor's harmless gesture rather than anything real. Henry Beecher pushed it into science after working as an army anaesthetist in the Second World War, where morphine ran short and he saw wounded soldiers get relief from injections of salt water. His 1955 paper argued that trials without a dummy comparison could not be trusted — which is why every serious drug trial now has one.

title: We Can Predict Gravity, Not Explain It
hook: Gravity is the force we understand best in practice and worst in principle.
story: Newton gave us an equation that predicts falling apples, orbits and tides with great accuracy, and he was honest that he had no idea what gravity actually is. He wrote that he framed no hypotheses about its cause. The equation worked; the mechanism was left open.

Einstein replaced it with a picture rather than a force. Mass and energy bend the shape of space and time around them, and objects simply travel the straightest available path through that bent geometry. The Earth is not being pulled by the Sun; it is following a straight line through curved space. This predicts things Newton could not — light bending around the Sun, clocks running slower near mass, ripples in space from colliding black holes, all since measured.

But that picture refuses to sit alongside the other great theory. Quantum mechanics describes the other three forces as exchanges of particles and works superbly at small scales. Every attempt to describe gravity the same way produces nonsense answers when pushed. The two theories are each nearly perfect in their own territory and contradict each other where the territories meet.

So we cannot say what gravity is at the smallest scale, or what happens at the centre of a black hole, or in the first instant of the universe. Serious attempts exist — string theory and loop quantum gravity among them — and none has yet made a prediction anyone has been able to test.
wow: Gravity is by far the weakest of the four forces. A small magnet lifts a paperclip against the pull of the entire planet.

quiz.q: How did Einstein describe gravity?
a: As the bending of space and time

quiz.q: What is the unsolved problem?
a: Gravity does not fit with quantum mechanics
Gravity is too strong to measure
